learningObjective: Distinguish dominance and post-dominance relations and identify implications for SSA construction and code motion.
stem: Which statements about dominance and post-dominance in a CFG with a distinguished entry are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Block D dominates block N (written D dom N) iff every path from the entry to N passes through D; the dominance relation forms a tree rooted at the entry block.

Block P post-dominates block N iff every path from N to the exit passes through P; post-dominance uses a reverse CFG and requires a distinguished exit (which may need to be synthesized for functions with multiple returns).
Dominance and post-dominance are the same relation; the two are equivalent for any well-formed CFG.
Dominance implies reachability from the entry, so unreachable code is not part of any dominator subtree and is typically removed before SSA construction.

explanation: A: standard dominance definition; the dominance relation forms a tree (dominator tree). B: post-dominance is the dual on the reverse CFG; a distinguished exit node is required for a well-defined post-dominance tree (synthesized when multiple returns exist). C is false: dominance and post-dominance are duals but not identical; e.g., a block may dominate itself trivially, but post-dominance depends on the exit structure. D is correct: unreachable code has no path from entry to it, so it is outside the dominator tree; DCE typically eliminates it first.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: dominance definition and tree property.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: post-dominance is the dual over reverse CFG requiring an exit.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: they are duals, not identities; they coincide only in trivial CFGs.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: unreachable code is excluded from the dominator tree and typically pruned first.

assumptions: CFG has a distinguished entry; for post-dominance, an exit (possibly synthesized) is added.
Standard textbook definitions from EAC3, Appel.
nonImplications: Does not imply that dominance is easy to compute; efficient algorithms (Lengauer-Tarjan) require some care.
Does not imply post-dominance is only useful for reverse analyses; sink-based optimizations and control dependence use it heavily.
